title: What mandated reporter training do US school employees need?
description: Statutory mandated reporter training for school staff in Pennsylvania (Act 126: 3 hours every 5 years) and Illinois (initial in 3 months, then every 3 years).
shortAnswer: Each state sets its own rule. In Pennsylvania, section 1205.6 of the Public School Code (Act 126 of 2012) requires school entities and their independent contractors to give employees with direct contact with children at least three hours of child abuse recognition and reporting training every five years. In Illinois, the Abused and Neglected Child Reporting Act requires mandated reporters, including school personnel, to train within three months of starting and at least every three years after.
keyTakeaways: Pennsylvania: 24 P.S. 12-1205.6 requires a minimum of three hours every five years for school employees with direct contact with children, covering four set topics, and applies to public, charter, cyber charter, private and nonpublic schools.
Pennsylvania school employees are mandated reporters under 23 Pa.C.S. 6311(a)(4); willful failure to report is a second degree misdemeanor and can be a third degree felony under 23 Pa.C.S. 6319.

Illinois: 325 ILCS 5/4, as reproduced in the Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) Manual for Mandated Reporters, requires initial training within three months of engagement and at least every three years after, with each reporter keeping completion records.
Illinois employers must have each employee sign a mandated reporter acknowledgment before starting work and keep it permanently in the personnel record.
The two states differ on who carries the duty: Pennsylvania puts it on the school entity, Illinois puts it on the individual reporter, so school records need to be designed for each.
regulator: Pennsylvania Department of Education and Department of Human Services; Illinois Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS)
appliesTo: Pennsylvania public, charter, cyber charter, private and nonpublic schools, intermediate units and area career and technical schools
Independent contractors of Pennsylvania school entities and their employees with direct contact with children
Illinois school personnel, including administrators and certified and non-certified school employees, and personnel of institutions of higher education
Human resources, compliance and professional development staff who track completion

sections.heading: Is mandated reporter training for school staff set federally or by each state?

blocks.text: By each state. Who must report child abuse, how, and what training they need are set in state statutes, so a district or school network operating in more than one state needs a separate rule set per state. This page covers two states whose statutes set specific hours or intervals for school staff: Pennsylvania and Illinois. Australian readers should use the separate page on [mandatory reporting training in Australia](/regulations/mandatory-reporting-training-australia), which follows different laws.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the Pennsylvania statutes and the Illinois DCFS materials as at November 2026. The Illinois training rule is quoted from the DCFS Manual for Mandated Reporters (September 2020 revised edition), which reproduces 325 ILCS 5/4; the Illinois General Assembly site was unavailable when this page was checked, so confirm the current statute text before relying on it.

sections.heading: What does Pennsylvania's Act 126 require of schools?

blocks.text: Pennsylvania requires school entities and their independent contractors to train every employee who has direct contact with children for at least three hours every five years. The rule is section 1205.6 of the [Public School Code of 1949](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/unconsolidated/law-information/view-statute?txtType=HTM&SessYr=1949&ActNum=0014.&SessInd=0&iFrame=true), added by Act 126 of July 5, 2012. Subsection (a) opens: "School entities and independent contractors of school entities shall provide their employes who have direct contact with children with mandatory training on child abuse recognition and reporting."
Section 1205.6(a)(1) sets four minimum topics:

items: Recognition of the signs of abuse and sexual misconduct, and reporting requirements for suspected abuse and sexual misconduct in Pennsylvania.
The Professional Educator Discipline Act, including its mandatory reporting requirements.
The school entity's own policies on reporting suspected abuse and sexual misconduct.
Maintenance of professional and appropriate relationships with students.

blocks.text: Training may be delivered online or by other distance systems (a)(2). Employees who must complete continuing professional education under section 1205.2 get credit for it if the program has been approved by the Department of Education in consultation with the Department of Public Welfare, which Act 132 of 2014 renamed the Department of Human Services (a)(4).

The definitions in subsection (b) set the scope. "School entity" covers a public school, charter school, cyber charter school, private school, nonpublic school, intermediate unit or area career and technical school. "Direct contact with children" means "the possibility of care, supervision, guidance or control of children or routine interaction with children", which brings in many non-teaching roles. The definition of "sexual misconduct", amended on October 30, 2019, lists grooming behaviors such as dating or soliciting dates and engaging in sexualized or romantic dialog.

sections.heading: Who must report in Pennsylvania, and what are the penalties?

blocks.text: Every school employee in Pennsylvania is a mandated reporter. [23 Pa.C.S. 6311(a)(4)](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=23&div=0&chapter=63&sctn=11&subsctn=0) lists "A school employee" among the adults who must report when they have reasonable cause to suspect a child is a victim of child abuse, and paragraph (13) separately lists an independent contractor.

Under [23 Pa.C.S. 6319](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=23&div=0&chapter=63&sctn=19&subsctn=0), willful failure to report is a misdemeanor of the second degree. It becomes a felony of the third degree where the abuse is a first degree felony or higher and the person has direct knowledge of its nature, and continuing failure to report or repeat offenses raise the grade further. The limitation period is the longer of the period for the underlying crime or five years.

School nurses, counselors and others who also hold a license from a Department of State board face a second rule. [23 Pa.C.S. 6383(b)(3)](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=23&div=0&chapter=63&sctn=83&subsctn=0) requires three hours of approved training for a new license and two hours of continuing education per renewal cycle. Section 6383(b)(4) lets a board exempt a person who has completed equal or greater training under section 1205.6 of the Public School Code, so one well documented Act 126 course can serve both requirements.

sections.heading: What does Illinois require of school personnel?

blocks.text: Illinois requires each mandated reporter, including school personnel, to complete initial training within three months of starting in the role and at least every three years after. The [DCFS Manual for Mandated Reporters](https://dcfs.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/dcfs/documents/safe-kids/reporting-child-abuse-and-neglect/documents/cfs-1050-21-mandated-reporter-manual.pdf) quotes 325 ILCS 5/4: reporters "must complete an initial mandated reporter training within three months of their date of engagement in a professional or official capacity as a mandated reporter ... and at least every three years thereafter".

The manual lists education personnel as mandated reporters, including "school personnel (including administrators and certified and non-certified school employees)", personnel of institutions of higher education, and truant officers. Training may be in person or web based and must cover, at minimum:

items: Indicators for recognizing child abuse and neglect as defined under the Act.
The Illinois reporting process and the required documentation.
Responding to a child in a trauma-informed manner.
The response of child protective services and the reporter's role after a call.

blocks.text: Training may come from DCFS, the State Board of Education, other listed public bodies, a continuing education provider approved by the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation, or a DCFS approved organization, and DCFS must offer a free web based course. Since January 1, 2021, the training counts toward continuing education hours for reporters licensed by that Department or the State Board of Education. A joint DCFS and Illinois State Board of Education [letter to school personnel](https://dcfs.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/dcfs/documents/safe-kids/reporting-child-abuse-and-neglect/documents/joint-dcfs-isbe-letter-to-school-personnel-081326.pdf) announced a fully redesigned course that adds guidance on distinguishing poverty from neglect, implicit bias, and a trauma-informed approach.

sections.heading: What records and penalties apply in Illinois?

blocks.text: Illinois puts the record keeping duty on the individual and a separate acknowledgment duty on the employer. Under 325 ILCS 5/4 as quoted in the manual, each reporter "shall report to his or her employer and, when applicable, to his or her licensing or certification board that he or she received the mandated reporter training" and "shall maintain records of completion".

Employees who became mandated reporters by virtue of their employment on or after July 1, 1986 must sign a statement, on a DCFS form provided by the employer, acknowledging the duty to report. The statement must be signed before employment begins and kept by the employer "as a permanent part of the personnel record".

A mandated reporter other than a physician who willfully fails to report is guilty of a Class A misdemeanor for a first violation and a Class 4 felony for a second or later violation (325 ILCS 5/4.02, as quoted in the manual). Physicians, dentists and dental hygienists are also referred to their disciplinary boards.

blocks.text: Rolling five year and three year cycles are easy to lose track of when staff join mid year, so tie each person's next due date to their own completion date rather than a school wide calendar, as described in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How should a school build training that meets these statutes?

blocks.text: Start from the statutory topic lists and add the school's own procedure, because both states require local content. Pennsylvania names "the school entity's policies related to reporting" as a required topic, and Illinois requires training on the reporting process and documentation, which depends on how the school routes reports internally while still making sure the individual reporter calls the hotline or the state agency.

items: **Separate the state course from the local module.** State approved or DCFS courses cover the law; a short local module covers who to tell internally, how to document, and how to support the child.
**Assess decisions, not recall.** Scenario questions about reasonable cause to suspect and the timing of a report show competence better than definitions do.
**Cover contractors.** Pennsylvania places the duty on independent contractors of school entities, so contracts for transport, food service and coaching should require proof of completion.

**Keep evidence per person.** Hours, topics, dates and acknowledgments should be retrievable for any employee, which is the standard in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

blocks.text: Colleges and universities in Illinois should note that personnel of institutions of higher education are listed mandated reporters, which places this training beside [Title IX](/regulations/title-ix-training-requirements) and [Clery Act](/regulations/clery-act-training-requirements) obligations in the [higher education](/industries/higher-education) compliance calendar.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each state's statutory topics, hours and intervals as separate obligations, links them to the roles they apply to, and defines the assessment point for each before content is written. A multi-state operator can then see which topics are shared, which are state specific, and which staff are due for renewal under which statute.

faqs.q: Does Pennsylvania's three hour requirement apply to private and religious schools?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 1205.6 defines a school entity to include private and nonpublic schools as well as public, charter and cyber charter schools, intermediate units and area career and technical schools. Their employees with direct contact with children need at least three hours every five years.

faqs.q: Can Act 126 training be done online?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 1205.6(a)(2) allows school entities and independent contractors to provide the training through the Internet or other distance communication systems. To earn continuing professional education credit, the program must be approved by the Department of Education in consultation with the Department of Human Services.

faqs.q: Who holds the training record in Illinois, the school or the employee?
faqs.a: The statute places the record on the employee: each mandated reporter must tell the employer, and any licensing board, that training was completed and must keep records of completion. Most schools also keep a copy, because the employer is the one asked to show compliance and must keep the signed acknowledgment form permanently.

faqs.q: Do substitute teachers and volunteers need the training?
faqs.a: In Pennsylvania the duty covers employees with direct contact with children, so employed substitutes are included; volunteers are not named in section 1205.6, though 23 Pa.C.S. 6311 can make some unpaid program staff mandated reporters. In Illinois the duty follows the mandated reporter role. Check each person's status against the statute.

faqs.q: Does reporting to the principal satisfy the duty to report?
faqs.a: Not by itself in either state. Illinois requires the reporter to immediately report or cause a report to be made to DCFS. Pennsylvania requires the mandated reporter to make the report under 23 Pa.C.S. 6313. Training should make clear that internal notification is in addition to, not instead of, the statutory report.
